title: Enhancing variational quantum classiﬁer performance with meta-heuristic feature selection for credit card fraud detection
journal_or_venue: The European Physical Journal Special Topics
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a hybrid quantum-classical framework that combines a variational quantum classifier (VQC) with traditional and meta-heuristic feature selection methods (PSO, ACO, ASO) and data balancing techniques (SMOTE-ENN, RUS) for credit card fraud detection on the European Cardholder dataset. Experiments using PennyLane quantum simulators show that PSO+VQC achieves the best performance (94.54% accuracy), with the authors noting limitations due to simulation-based evaluation and recommending future validation on real quantum hardware.
methodology_description: The study implements a hybrid classical–quantum classification pipeline for credit-card fraud detection. It uses the publicly available European Cardholder credit card fraud dataset. After removing duplicate records, the minority fraud class was augmented using SMOTE and cleaned with ENN (SMOTE-ENN) and then class balance was achieved using Random Under Sampling (RUS) to create a balanced dataset (25,000 non-fraud / 25,000 fraud). Multiple feature-selection methods were applied independently: traditional filter-based K-Best and three meta-heuristics (Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), and Atom Search Optimization (ASO)). Each selected feature subset was used to train a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) implemented and simulated in PennyLane on a classical workstation. The VQC pipeline used amplitude encoding to map classical features into quantum states, applied a parameterized quantum circuit U_theta (gates parameterized by learnable parameters), measured the first qubit S times to estimate class probabilities, added a learnable bias term and thresholded at 0.5 for binary output. Models were trained on 37,500 samples and tested on 12,500 samples. Performance was reported using accuracy, precision, recall and F1 score. PSO + VQC achieved the best reported result (accuracy 94.54%).
experimental_setup: Simulated VQC experiments were run on a classical workstation using the PennyLane framework. The classical machine specs were: CPU AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, GPU NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3050, 16 GB RAM, Windows 10 Pro. No real QPU was used; all quantum circuits were executed in simulation.
dataset_used: European Cardholder credit-card transactions dataset (publicly available via Kaggle / Machine Learning Group ULB & Worldline). Initially 284,807 transactions with severe class imbalance (≈0.17% fraud). Dataset contains 29 anonymized features plus Time and Amount.

experiment_input.source: European Cardholder Dataset (Machine Learning Group, ULB / Worldline) hosted on Kaggle

augmentation_and_balancing.description: Minority fraud class oversampled from 473 up to 283,253 synthetic minority samples
Edited Nearest Neighbors applied to remove noisy samples; total after ENN reported as 282,801 for minority class
Total dataset after SMOTE-ENN reported as 566,054 (combined)
Random under-sampling of majority class to 25,000 and balancing with 25,000 fraud samples to create final balanced dataset of 50,000

experiment_process: Pipeline steps: 1) Data cleaning (duplicate removal). 2) Data augmentation with SMOTE and noise cleaning with ENN (SMOTE-ENN). 3) Random under-sampling to generate a balanced dataset (25k/25k). 4) Apply feature selection methods independently (K-Best, PSO, ACO, ASO) to obtain feature subsets. 5) Encode selected classical feature vectors into quantum states using amplitude encoding. 6) Process encoded states with a parameterized quantum model circuit U_theta (parameterized gates G(α,β,γ,φ)). 7) Measure the first qubit S times to estimate the Bernoulli probability p(q0=1|x;θ). 8) Add a learnable bias term b, threshold π(x;θ,b)>0.5 to obtain binary prediction. 9) Train/update parameters using a classical optimizer (unspecified) in the PennyLane simulation environment. 10) Evaluate on held-out test set and report accuracy, precision, recall, F1. Note: The paper specifies amplitude encoding, parameterized gate form, measurement-and-bias postprocessing, and that the circuit is executed S times for probability estimation. Specific optimizer type, learning rate, number of training iterations/epochs, qubit count, circuit depth and shot count (S) are not reported.

experiment_output.baselines: Comparison was between the feature-selection methods paired with the same VQC model. No classical ML baseline metrics (e.g., Random Forest) are provided in the reported results in this paper.

hardware_details.simulator: PennyLane (quantum circuit simulation on classical hardware)

reproducibility_notes: Data: The European Cardholder dataset is publicly available (Kaggle / Machine Learning Group ULB & Worldline). Code: The paper does not provide a code repository or explicit hyperparameter settings. The implementation used PennyLane for simulated VQC; SMOTE-ENN and RUS were applied (library not specified). Missing details for exact reproduction: qubit count, circuit architecture depth, number of shots S, classical optimizer type and hyperparameters, training epochs/iterations, random seeds. To reproduce, one would need to reimplement the VQC described (amplitude encoding, parameterized gates of form G(α,β,γ,φ), measurement-and-bias postprocessing), apply the same data cleaning and balancing steps (SMOTE-ENN then RUS to 25k/25k), and run feature selection (K-Best, PSO, ACO, ASO) to obtain the listed feature subsets. Because the key training hyperparameters are not reported and no code is provided, exact numeric replication may not be possible without contacting the authors for details.
key_findings: [supported] PSO+VQC achieved 94.54% accuracy (precision 93.64%, recall 93.55%, F1 0.9359) on the balanced (50,000) European Cardholder dataset using SMOTE-ENN + RUS and PennyLane simulator.
[supported] ACO+VQC achieved 89.70% accuracy (precision 84.49%, recall 88.47%, F1 0.8644) in the same experimental setup.
[supported] ASO+VQC achieved 89.12% accuracy (precision 91.64%, recall 87.15%, F1 0.8934) in the same experimental setup.
[supported] K-Best (traditional feature selection) + VQC achieved 84.48% accuracy (precision 99.17%, recall 47.57%, F1 0.6441) in the same experimental setup.

[supported] The authors used SMOTE-ENN to oversample the minority class and Random Under Sampler to produce a 25k/25k class-balanced dataset (total 50,000), with a 75/25 train/test split (37,500/12,500).
[supported] Experiments were run on quantum simulators (PennyLane) executed on classical hardware (AMD Ryzen 7 5800H, NVIDIA RTX 3050, 16GB RAM).

[supported] In these experiments, meta-heuristic feature selection (PSO, ACO, ASO) combined with a VQC produced better classification performance than the K-Best filter method; PSO+VQC produced the best results among tested methods.

[supported] The paper explicitly notes limitations: results are from simulators and may not reflect real quantum hardware performance due to noise, decoherence, gate/qubit constraints, and limited access to real devices.

[speculative] The authors claim that QML (VQC) reduces dependence on large datasets and better adapts to dynamic processes than classical ML (this is asserted theoretically but not demonstrated empirically in the paper).

[speculative] The authors present the simulator results as precursors to running on real quantum computers and suggest that future tests on real hardware (e.g., IBM devices) could improve results; this is a projection, not demonstrated.

[disputed] The paper makes a broader claim that QML + meta-heuristic approaches can surpass conventional methods and deliver superior accuracy/efficiency; this is contradicted by classical benchmarks cited within the paper (multiple classical studies report >98% accuracy on the same/related dataset) and is therefore disputed as a general claim.
results_summary: The paper reports a hybrid pipeline for credit card fraud detection that uses SMOTE-ENN + random undersampling to balance the European Cardholder dataset, multiple feature selection methods (K-Best, PSO, ACO, ASO), and a Variational Quantum Classifier simulated with PennyLane. Empirically, PSO combined with the VQC produced the best simulated performance (94.54% accuracy, precision 93.64%, recall 93.55%), outperforming the other tested feature-selection+VQC combinations (ACO 89.70%, ASO 89.12%, K-Best 84.48%). Experiments ran on classical hardware via a quantum simulator; the authors note simulator-based limitations and propose future testing on real quantum devices. They also make broader, less-supported claims about QML’s potential advantages over classical methods.
performance_claims: Data balancing: minority class oversampled via SMOTE-ENN and majority reduced via RUS to form a 50,000-sample balanced dataset (25,000 non-fraud, 25,000 fraud).
Train/test split: 37,500 training samples, 12,500 test samples.
quantum_advantage_detail: The authors assert potential advantages of QML (VQC) for fraud detection and show promising simulator results (PSO+VQC at 94.54% accuracy). However, experiments were performed on simulators (no real quantum hardware), and the paper lacks head-to-head comparisons to strong classical baselines within the same experimental setup (and cites classical studies with higher accuracies). Thus any claimed quantum advantage remains speculative rather than demonstrated.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Proposes a hybrid classical–quantum pipeline combining meta-heuristic feature selection (PSO/ACO/ASO), data balancing (SMOTE-ENN + RUS) and a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) simulated in PennyLane; PSO + VQC achieved the best reported accuracy (94.54%).

#idea:quantum-ml — Applies a VQC (amplitude encoding, parameterized circuit, measurement + bias thresholding) to a heavily preprocessed credit-card fraud dataset and reports standard classification metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, confusion matrices).

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Uses a variational NISQ-style classifier and discusses the need for future validation on real quantum hardware, indicating an eye toward near-term quantum workflows but stopping short of hardware demonstration.
#limitation:simulation-only — All quantum experiments are performed on a PennyLane simulator on classical hardware; no experiments on real QPUs were conducted.

#limitation:no-empirical-validation — Authors acknowledge limitations of simulation-only evaluation and recommend validation on real quantum hardware (no noise/imperfection effects were empirically studied).

#limitation:qubit-count — Key implementation details (qubit count, circuit depth, shot count, optimizer type, learning rate, training iterations) are not reported, reducing reproducibility and preventing assessment of scalability to real devices.
#limitation:data-encoding — Uses amplitude encoding to load classical features but does not discuss the resource or computational cost of state preparation for realistic feature sizes.
#limitation:noise — Because experiments are noise-free simulations, the impact of hardware noise and error mitigation on classifier performance is unaddressed.
